analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from sharing rent data through pricing software that coordinates rents.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 37 House Democrats behind it and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill makes it a crime under antitrust law for landlords to hire a company that collects rent, lease, and vacancy data from multiple landlords and uses software to recommend what each of them should charge. That practice — often done through rent-setting software — is already the subject of government lawsuits; this bill would write a flat ban into statute, let the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general enforce it, and let overcharged tenants sue for triple damages. It has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, especially the roughly 44 million US renter households, who would pay rents set by their own landlord's judgment rather than by prices coordinated across competing landlords.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters in markets with algorithmic pricing

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a per se Sherman Act violation for any landlord to pay for a 'coordinator' service — one that collects rents, lease dates, and vacancy data from multiple owners and recommends prices, lease terms, or occupancy targets [S2].
It bans the coordinating service itself, so the software company performing the function is liable alongside the landlords who buy it [S2].
It gives renters a private right of action with tripled damages, attorney's fees, and interest, and invalidates pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers for claims under the Act [S2].
It makes the conduct enforceable by the FTC, the Attorney General, and every state attorney general, using existing antitrust enforcement powers [S2].
It lowers the pleading bar so rent-fixing complaints cannot be dismissed merely for failing to rule out that each landlord acted independently, a common early exit for antitrust suits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords using coordinated pricing software, and the companies that sell it. Whether savings flow to tenants depends on competitive conditions in each rental market.

drawbacks.text: The ban is written as a flat per se rule, so even a landlord's own use of a standard pricing tool for its own portfolio could count as an unlawful 'coordinating function,' since the definition includes 'a rental property owner performing a coordinating function for their own benefit' [S2].

Critics of rent-fixing lawsuits argue that software recommends prices but landlords can and do reject them, so the practice is ordinary pricing, not price fixing; that argument is being tested in ongoing federal litigation rather than resolved by Congress.
Supporters and opponents agree housing costs are driven largely by a shortage of homes; a ban on coordinated pricing would not build a single unit, so rents in tight markets could remain high.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If coordinated pricing does push rents above competitive levels, the bill directly targets that practice and gives overcharged tenants a way to recover. The main risk is overbreadth: the per se ban sweeps in some pricing software that a landlord uses on its own portfolio, and the added uncertainty could chill ordinary revenue management without delivering much rent relief in supply-starved markets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 19, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it currently sits with no further action [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Becca Balint introduced the bill with 14 original cosponsors on November 19, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S2] [S4].
It has attracted 36 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The bill has no committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote recorded after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, no outcome has been reached. Rental-pricing software firms and large landlords continue operating under the current legal regime, where coordination cases must be litigated case by case rather than facing the flat statutory ban this bill would create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; status quo persists

for.name: Rep. Becca Balint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 36 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

for.name: U.S. Department of Justice Antitrust Division
for.what_they_did: Brought a civil antitrust suit alleging that a leading rent-setting software provider and major landlords conspired to keep rents high, the same practice this bill would ban by statute.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee of a Republican-controlled House without further action [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Rent-setting software providers (e.g. RealPage-style revenue management firms)
industries.note: Their core business — pooling rent, lease, and vacancy data across landlords and recommending prices — would become a per se antitrust violation, and their landlord contracts would be unlawful to buy. The bill would end a revenue stream built on servicing multiple competing landlords at once.

industries.industry: Large landlords and institutional property managers
industries.note: They could no longer subscribe to shared pricing services, and paying for one would itself be illegal. Small landlords that set rents independently would be largely untouched.

Renters in markets where landlords share data through a common pricing platform would gain a statutory ban and a private right of action with triple damages and an escape from pre-dispute arbitration for these claims.

analysis.trajectory: A new bill with only Democratic cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, sitting in committee with no action scheduled, is unlikely to advance this session; the practical fight over algorithmic rent-setting is instead playing out in ongoing antitrust litigation and agency actions.
